title: Extreme heat turns energy affordability into a safety, health, and policy-targeting problem
source_unit: Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability report, The Cost of Keeping Cool: Energy Affordability and Extreme Heat
geography: United States; county-level household energy-cost and energy-poverty estimates

observations.period: 2026; household energy affordability and extreme heat

denominator.unit: national report using county-level estimates of household energy costs and energy poverty

energy_burden_geography.value: energy burden is mapped across the country and varies by region and season

cooling_cost_focus.value: the report treats cooling costs during extreme heat as a distinct component of household energy affordability

observations.method: Report synthesis using county-level estimates of household energy costs and energy poverty, with regional and seasonal analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not provide the underlying county estimates, model specification, or individual household outcomes; mapped burden is not a direct measure of any one household's bill or health outcome.
observations.subgroup: Households facing energy poverty, high cooling needs, rising electricity costs, and different regional or seasonal heat exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Regional variation can reflect climate, housing, prices, appliance efficiency, income, and energy assistance; a high modeled burden does not identify a single cause or prove service disconnection.

denominator.unit: report-level account of safe-home functions requiring consistent electricity

electricity_as_safety_input.value: consistent electricity is necessary to preserve or prepare food, charge medical devices, and heat or cool living spaces

tradeoff.value: unaffordable bills force choices between maintaining a safe and comfortable home and meeting other needs

observations.method: Report framing of energy affordability as a household safety condition rather than only a price measure.
observations.uncertainty: The report description does not estimate the prevalence, dollar size, or duration of these tradeoffs; it does not establish that every unaffordable bill produces the same adaptation or harm.
observations.subgroup: Households dependent on electricity for food, medical-device charging, heating, cooling, and other basic domestic functions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Households may draw on savings, community support, payment plans, efficiency improvements, or assistance; the source identifies a risk mechanism, not a universal outcome.

denominator.unit: report-level interaction between heat exposure and household energy affordability

compounding_pressure.value: rising temperatures and increasing electricity costs place additional pressure on households already struggling with energy affordability

heat_amplification.value: high temperatures intensify the consequences of energy insecurity

observations.method: Report analysis connecting energy-burden geography and seasonal variation to extreme-heat and cooling-cost exposure.
observations.uncertainty: The source description establishes a compounding mechanism but does not identify a causal effect size, threshold, or household-level response sequence.
observations.subgroup: Energy-insecure households in places and seasons with high cooling demand, especially households with health or housing constraints.
observations.counterinterpretation: Weatherization, efficient cooling, shade, community cooling, and lower-cost generation can reduce exposure; heat does not mechanically produce unaffordable energy for every household.

denominator.unit: report assessment of federal and state energy-affordability support

cooling_access_blind_spot.value: existing federal and state energy-affordability support fails to recognize the importance of cooling access

policy_design_implication.value: reducing household energy burden requires incorporating the compounding role of extreme heat

observations.method: Report assessment of energy-affordability support against the safety and cooling requirements created by extreme heat.
observations.uncertainty: This is a report conclusion, not an independent program evaluation; the abstract does not enumerate all programs, eligibility rules, take-up, or implementation outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Households eligible for or excluded from energy assistance, state and federal administrators, utilities, and communities exposed to extreme heat.
observations.counterinterpretation: Programs may address cooling indirectly through bill support, weatherization, or emergency response; the claimed gap may differ across jurisdictions and program designs.

related_sources.claim: Climate Central supplies a separate U.S. heat-related emergency-visit and climate-attribution route; it is retained as a distinct health-outcome source.
Annenberg supplies a separate public-experience, routine, and cooling-center-awareness route; it is retained as a distinct survey source.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. energy-affordability route linking county-level energy burden, electricity-dependent household safety, extreme-heat compounding, cooling access, and policy design. It is a report synthesis based on modeled county estimates and an abstract-level source description; it does not establish individual bills, clinical outcomes, disconnections, assistance take-up, causal effect sizes, or policy effectiveness.
